invariants.why: One WebSocket JSON-RPC client is shared by every page. A second transport, or a rename, must be declared here deliberately rather than absorbed by the graph.
Every calling surface competes for the same pool and socket. A surface that reaches the gateway some other way breaks the concurrent-access picture the graph draws.

The pool is the transport's only shared mutable state: every mutation happens under the lock, continuations resume and frames are written outside it. The critical-section assembly assumes exactly this shape.
If the register, resolve or remove rules stop matching the source, the pool must fail the build rather than look idle.
Sections are assembled per enclosing function; an operation with no resolved scope would silently drop out of its section.
Every namespace box is dispatched by a transport core; a namespace reached any other way is a new construction, not a variant of this one.
Every store the extractor recognises is a construction on the map, so the System map can never disagree with the extractor about what holds state.

Every page's views drive at least one surface through an observed action or lifecycle hook. SwiftUI has many ways to attach an action; if a refactor hides them from the rules, the first hop must fail loudly rather than vanish.

The App entry points construct the objects that exist before any page: the settings object reads the keychain in its initialiser and is what the transport connects with. A store read only at launch belongs to the launch zone, not to the shared core; if the @StateObject or init rules stop matching, launch must fail loudly rather than dissolve into shared.

An object's lifecycle is the enum its stored state property is typed with, and every state must be reachable by an assignment somewhere in the type. Adding, renaming or orphaning a state changes the construction and must be declared here in the same change; a state nothing ever enters is dead code the map would otherwise draw as live.

A system flow is a path over edges the map draws, never a diagram beside it. When the construction changes under a flow, the flow must be updated in the same change rather than quietly describing wiring that no longer exists.
Every declared page owns at least one construct. An empty page means its roots or ownership declarations have drifted from the source.

lint_rules.message: Use Logger from os.log instead of NSLog
Don't swallow errors with `try?` — it discards the error and yields nil with no log or branch. Use do/catch to handle it, or `try` to propagate.
Use Logger from os.log instead of print(); print goes to stdout with no level or subsystem and can't be filtered in Console or silenced in release.
Views must not call the raw GatewayClient; go through a ViewModel or accept an AgentBackend (see PR #190 — hardwired views broke Centaur sessions).
Services are the platform-agnostic layer — no SwiftUI. Use Foundation/Combine; presentation concerns belong in Views or ViewModels.
No new singletons — `.shared` is invisible coupling that can't be swapped in tests. Inject the dependency through an initializer or the environment instead.

Synchronous file I/O on the main thread causes a beachball — read files in Task.detached (or a background actor) and await the result. See the main-thread hang watchdog in architecture-rules.md for the detection story.
Route user-facing errors through an error-mapping helper; raw strings become red banners (advisory warnings must not look like failures — see #191/#192).

Don't wrap a timer .onReceive's state write in withAnimation — it queues an animation transaction every tick and beachballs during streaming (#252). Assign plainly (the redraw is the animation) and gate the timer to idle.

Heavy pure work (parse/extract/build/link/compose/highlight) in a computed view property re-runs every render and stalls the main thread (#210/#217). Memoize via RenderMemo, or compute once in init — not per body evaluation.

Don't combine @Observable with ObservableObject — they register two separate observation mechanisms and can double-notify or miss updates. Remove ObservableObject and migrate callers to @Bindable / @Observable access (#262).
Don't use DispatchQueue.main inside a @MainActor ViewModel — the hop escapes actor ownership tracking. Call directly, or use Task { @MainActor in } / Task.sleep for deferred work (#262).

Compare a generation counter with == / != , not ordering (<, <=, >, >=). A generation is an identity token for "is this completion stale?", not a monotonic version — ordering comparisons admit stale results the == guard drops. (Version-number last-writer-wins, à la ArtifactStore.rev, is a different idiom — use a field named `rev`/`version`, not `generation`.)

ObservableObject classes must be @MainActor — SwiftUI observes objectWillChange on the main thread; a mutation from any other context is an unsynchronized write. Add @MainActor to the class declaration (#262).

semantic.summary: Living artifact presentation. ArtifactKindRenderer is the one place that decides how an artifact of any kind is drawn and — for interactive HTML — whether the host captures the mouse for it. The renderer's contract for live artifacts is that the action manifest travels with the artifact id: an html artifact declares its intents on the record rather than in its content, so passing actionableArtifactID without topLevelActions injects the intent bridge, captures the click, and resolves it against an empty manifest — the exact shape of a regression that left every control dead in the macOS side panel (the primary way an artifact is opened) and the iOS sheet while the expanded overlay worked. The surfaces that open a live artifact forward both: the transcript panel, the iOS artifact sheet, the expanded overlay, and the fullscreen window's intent context. Inline intent clicks are gated twice in the host — the negotiated capability set must advertise an artifact.action surface, and the binding must resolve against the declared manifest — and both refusals are logged at notice, because the page has already swallowed the click and a dead control otherwise looks identical to missing markup. Status display prefers the unsupported reason over the generic harness sentence at every site: the renderer's inline status row and the fullscreen window's status line both show IntentInvocationState's reason first, so copy names the gate that actually closed — a local miss, no connection, a gateway too old for the method, or a gateway verdict — instead of pointing at a server that was never asked. Status is also reflected back onto the page: every live intent slot for the artifact becomes a data-hermes-status mark, so each inert control reflects its own outcome independently of the one last clicked. HTML artifacts that declare actions but place no inline markers fall back to ArtifactTopLevelActionBar — trusted SwiftUI chrome above the document, no JS bridge involved. Blueprints enter the renderer's kind table the way every native block kind does: a ```blueprint fence or a stored blueprint artifact renders through BlueprintBlockView, which preserves the coordinates and dimensions its author declared on a logical canvas instead of asking a layout to infer placement — the deliberate opposite of the graph and Mermaid renderers, where the renderer owns geometry. The kind is registered at every site the other kinds are: ArtifactKindRenderer's dispatch, the ruler glyph in the canvas, fullscreen, transcript, panel, and thought-graph icon tables, and the structural preview gist that counts surviving elements and reads the title.

semantic.summary: The agent-execution dashboard: the flamechart, the session canvas that rearranges a live chat into per-turn lenses, the free-form panel canvas, and the conversation panel that renders the live transcript as one more dashboard panel. ThoughtGraphView is the interactive flamechart of the react loop — horizontal position is when a step happened, bar width is how long, each actor owns a lane stacked by spawn order — and carries an explicit legacy-giant header: split tracked as debt, do not add to the file. SessionChatCanvas drives lenses by CanvasDisplayMode: scroll streams the live turn, turns pages one settled turn at a time, and only the per-turn lenses and the conversation focus change between modes. DashboardCanvasView is deliberately content-agnostic — z-order is layout-array order, frames live in the canvas's own coordinate space, and layout persists via onLayoutCommitted on drag-end so UserDefaults writes stay off the per-frame path — and PanelContext hands every panel builder the same material: the turn's composed nodes, compaction folds, skills, the shared cross-highlight selection, and the single flamechart engine. The conversation panel's live tool calls are the newest load-bearing rule: ChatMessage.toolCalls is stamped once at message.complete, so during a running turn the records live only in ChatViewModel.activeToolCalls — mergingLiveToolCalls(into:activeToolCalls:) merges them into the streaming message before the peel bar and tools card are built, which is what makes the Tools chip and card exist while tools run instead of every tool appearing at once when the turn ends; the merge guards on message.isStreaming so a settled turn keeps its own stamped history rather than borrowing the next turn's in-flight records, and liveToolCallOrder sorts by startedAt with an id tiebreak because dictionary values rehash on every insert — sorting is what stops the rows reshuffling under the cursor on each tool event. Each turn's thinking and tools are peelable cards (PeeledBlockKind) anchored under the bubble — the card is the block's only render site, so the bubble is stripped of reasoning and the streaming status line does not re-list tools; nothing renders twice. The transcript is an eager VStack over a bounded 60-message tail window (lazy layout was the engine of a sampled 100%-CPU relayout loop), the live-tail follow is coalesced to one unanimated scroll per 150ms, and re-rendering is driven by ChatViewModel publishes, never a timer.

semantic.summary: The declared-intent contract for living artifacts: artifacts declare verbs as data, and clicks on inert markup dispatch real backend work. ArtifactAction is the declaration — local kinds (choice/toggle/delete) mutate content through the same upsert→push path agent writes use, while intent kinds carry a stable binding ID the gateway resolves against the pinned revision; the intent name travelling with the artifact is display and debugging material, never the thing to run. HTMLArtifactIntentBridge is the only way out of untrusted content: a trusted click on data-hermes-binding markup becomes a nonce-gated private-scheme navigation in an isolated content world — synthetic clicks rejected, no message handler, fetch, or credential exposed — and native mirrors status back onto data-hermes-status attributes in the same world with a closed token vocabulary the page can style but not forge. ArtifactStore owns dispatch: slots keyed artifact/binding/entity so sibling rows report independently, idempotency keys reused per slot so a retry cannot execute twice, confirmation challenges bound server-side to actor, revision, binding, and expiry, and ledger rehydration seeding only terminal outcomes without overwriting live in-session state. IntentInvocationState.unsupported carries a reason distinguishing the four ways no handler ran — the artifact isn't in the local store, no gateway connection, a gateway with no artifact.action.invoke method at all, and a successful round trip whose binding has no registered handler — and each refusal is logged at notice, because the page has already swallowed the click and a silent refusal is indistinguishable from a dead control. MaintainerRef separates an artifact a cron actively tends from one that is merely mutable, and ArtifactIntentSessionLink lets native chrome post the session switch for an intent that ran as a contained session — reusing the same in-process notification the sidebar and inbox use, never handing the untrusted page a session ID or any navigation capability. semantic.summary: Value types and wire/domain models shared across user experiences and service adapters. Cron job organization is modeled by CronCategory, which derives arbitrary-depth category paths from a job's own name and owns the display-name rules every surface shares. The dataflow graph now has an identity you can quote: CronGraphDigest is a SHA-256 content address over a canonical, byte-sorted, length-prefixed form of the graph as configured — schedule, enabled, usesLLM, deliver, description, and every edge are in, while lastStatus and health are out so the 10-second health poll cannot mint revisions — and layoutForm, a strict subset kept in the same file because the difference is the point, answers only whether a refresh must re-run the force layout. CronGraphRevisionStore keeps the append-on-change observation log: per-observation UUID identity so a revert A → B → A is three entries, runtime state stripped before storing so over(revision.graph) == revision.digest holds forever, capped at 200 revisions for disk. CronGraphDiff reports typed, human-phrased statements — rename versus refile told apart by leaf and path, edges as dataflow — with affectedNodeIDs, addedEdgeIDs, and removedEdges derived from the statements so the drawer and the canvas cannot drift. CronChangeset is the gateway-recorded counterpart carrying what the observed log structurally cannot: real time, an actor (human/agent/scheduler/other/unknown), and provenance turns. CronGraph itself is Codable for local snapshots only; gateway decoding stays on decodeGatewayValue. GatewayCapabilities is the negotiated-capability value the feature gates read: supportsArtifactActions, supportsActionLog, and supportsLearning hide their features when the set is silent, while supportsGatewayRestart is deliberately inverted — a gateway that reported nothing still gets the restart button, because restart is the recovery control and hiding it is how you end up needing shell access on the host; a gateway that did report and didn't list restart is taken at its word. The negotiated set is displayed by no view, so diagnosticSummary renders it as a pure, testable one-line verdict — the count, a loud supported/ABSENT artifact-actions flag, sorted names (or "none listed" so an empty set doesn't render as a bare colon) — which GatewayCapabilitiesStore logs at notice when capabilities resolve, the first place to look when a feature silently isn't there. BlueprintSpec is the wire contract for the same family's newest kind: the JSON body of a ```blueprint fence, decoded against a declared logical canvas (100 × 100 by default, each axis clamped to 10–1000) where every x/y/width/height is author-placed. Decoding is total where it can be — kind and style strings match case-insensitively and fall back to generic and flow — and sanitizing where integrity matters: element ids are trimmed with empties dropped and duplicates resolved first-wins, geometry clamps into the canvas with non-finite values collapsing to the minimum, and a connection survives only when both endpoints exist and differ. A spec whose elements all vanish parses as nil so the view shows its parse-error card instead of an empty drawing, and parsing is memoized through the shared RenderMemo (32 entries) like every other block spec. As a living artifact, a blueprint re-emit takes ArtifactMerge's default replace path — the incoming document replaces the stored one wholesale, the same semantics charts and timelines have.

semantic.summary: Reusable presentation primitives that no single product surface owns: chat skins, theme-aware controls, status surfaces, and presentation policy that stays testable without a running app. MacTopChrome is the pattern at its purest — a view-free enum whose one protected rule is that collapsing the chrome must never take the Back button away: mode(isSurfaceOpen:isCollapsed:) lets an open surface override the user's stored collapse preference because the surface header owns Back and its Escape shortcut, and height(for:) maps the mode to the 40pt expanded / 22pt collapsed row so callers never branch on the raw preference. invariants.why: One WebSocket JSON-RPC client is shared by every page. A second transport, or a rename, must be declared here deliberately rather than absorbed by the graph.
Every calling surface competes for the same pool and socket. A surface that reaches the gateway some other way breaks the concurrent-access picture the graph draws.

The pool is the transport's only shared mutable state: every mutation happens under the lock, continuations resume and frames are written outside it. The critical-section assembly assumes exactly this shape.
If the register, resolve or remove rules stop matching the source, the pool must fail the build rather than look idle.
Sections are assembled per enclosing function; an operation with no resolved scope would silently drop out of its section.
Every namespace box is dispatched by a transport core; a namespace reached any other way is a new construction, not a variant of this one.
Every store the extractor recognises is a construction on the map, so the System map can never disagree with the extractor about what holds state.

Every page's views drive at least one surface through an observed action or lifecycle hook. SwiftUI has many ways to attach an action; if a refactor hides them from the rules, the first hop must fail loudly rather than vanish.

The App entry points construct the objects that exist before any page: the settings object reads the keychain in its initialiser and is what the transport connects with. A store read only at launch belongs to the launch zone, not to the shared core; if the @StateObject or init rules stop matching, launch must fail loudly rather than dissolve into shared.

An object's lifecycle is the enum its stored state property is typed with, and every state must be reachable by an assignment somewhere in the type. Adding, renaming or orphaning a state changes the construction and must be declared here in the same change; a state nothing ever enters is dead code the map would otherwise draw as live.

A system flow is a path over edges the map draws, never a diagram beside it. When the construction changes under a flow, the flow must be updated in the same change rather than quietly describing wiring that no longer exists.
Every declared page owns at least one construct. An empty page means its roots or ownership declarations have drifted from the source.

nodes.overlay_prose: The in-flight attachment download pool. fetch(url:token:attachmentID:) registers a CheckedContinuation under the attachment's UUID and starts a URLSessionDownloadTask on the manager's own URLSession; the URLSessionDownloadDelegate callbacks resolve and remove it when the file lands or the task fails. Unlike the gateway pool it is not lock-guarded: the manager is @MainActor and the delegate hops back to it, so registration and resolution are serialised by the actor, not by a lock. It is a download pool, not an RPC pool, and never touches the gateway.
